summary:
Mississippi's own statutes, not the national framework, set the terms a trans visitor meets inside the state. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records that Mississippi enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and that state statute defines sex by birth. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people; the grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

A law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." A 2024 Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event. State law bars transgender students from school sports consistent with gender identity under SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, requiring any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA, and hormone levels.

Mississippi bans gender-affirming care for individuals under age 18 under the Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023. After the law's enactment, the University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic in the state.

Identity documents are a live exposure. The Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with new name and gender marker upon certified court order, medical statement attesting to gender reassignment, and fee, but the amended certificate lists both updated and original information. From 1 November 2021 to March 2026, a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed driver's license marker changes; a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth.

On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance, holding that a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest. A separate enacted measure prohibits inmate name changes after The Real You Act of 2022 died in committee.

State non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Federal Title VII per Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) prohibits employment discrimination based on gender identity. Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only.

The 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, but federal prosecution remains available under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale, a federal prosecution of a bias killing in Mississippi.

The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects refusal of services based on belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics. The law took effect after the Fifth Circuit lifted an injunction on 23 June 2017.

Two anti-trans bills died in the Mississippi legislature in 2024 after House and Senate lawmakers failed to reach agreement on compromise versions by the 29 April 2024 deadline: the SAFER Act, which would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the Women's Bill of Rights, which would have codified a binary definition of sex as determined at birth into state law and curtailed legal recognition of transgender people's gender identities. The SAFER Act had previously been supported by a House majority.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, overriding a 1996 executive order, 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 3 approved by 86.01% of voters; those bans remain unrepealed, and Attorney General Jim Hood on 29 June 2015 directed clerks to comply or face lawsuits after initial resistance. Mississippi banned adoption and fostering by same-sex couples in 2000 and was the only state still enforcing such a ban by 2015, until U.S. District Judge Daniel Porter Jordan III struck it down 31 March 2016 with final effect 2 May 2016 after no appeal.

Mississippi maintains HIV criminalization making failure to disclose HIV-positive status to a sexual partner a felony even without transmission, with at least 43 arrests for HIV-related offenses between 2004 and 2021 per a 2024 Williams Institute report. Mississippi's sodomy statute originating in 1839 with up to ten years' imprisonment remains on the books unenforceable following Lawrence v. Texas (2003), and persons convicted before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law, prompting a 2016 federal lawsuit by five residents and $400,000 in taxpayer legal fees reported in 2023.

For visible local climate, Starkville hosted its first pride parade 24 March 2018 after initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the city's history.
tangentialFactors:
A 2019 PRRI poll found that 68% of Mississippians favored laws that would protect gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing, and public accommodations, with 23% opposed. By 2024, PRRI reported support for such a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity reached 67%. Compared to national averages, Mississippi tends to show lower support for same-sex marriage and transgender rights, but opinion gaps have narrowed over time, with younger Mississippians showing significantly higher support for LGBTQ rights than older residents.

The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 grading of Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric, placing Mississippi among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people.

The 2024 legislative session saw two anti-trans bills die on the 29 April deadline despite prior House majority support for the SAFER Act, indicating legislative momentum that did not consolidate that session even as bathroom restrictions were enacted by other means in 2024 and 2025.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 "Worst Laws Passed" grading of Mississippi rests on a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric; the specific rubric weights and Mississippi's score are not reproduced in this record.

The April 2025 Mississippi Supreme Court name-change ruling is reported in one source as denying the petition outright and in another as permitting a name change only at age 21 for "lack of maturity"; both accounts agree on the 8-1 vote, the 17 April 2025 date, the misgendering in the majority opinion, and the citation of the REAP Act. The precise age condition is unresolved between sources.

Whether the March 2026 law prohibiting driver's license markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth has been challenged in court is not sourced here.

The 2024 Harrison County dress code incident involving a transgender girl threatened with in-school suspension is reported without a date beyond the year 2024; no later instance of dress-code enforcement against a trans student in Mississippi is documented in this record.

Whether federal Title VII enforcement under Bostock is actively pursued in Mississippi, and how the state's non-recognition of gender-identity protections interacts with federal claims in practice, is not sourced here.
